articles.title: Zambrero Opens New Mexican Restaurant on Mellor Street, Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Zambrero has launched its latest branch on Mellor Street, offering a menu of Mexican-inspired dishes and a commitment to donate meals to those in need.
articles.content_html:
A new Mexican restaurant, Zambrero, has opened its doors on Mellor Street in Rochdale. The restaurant launched at 11am on September 25, offering a diverse menu of Mexican-inspired dishes including burritos, bowls, tacos, nachos, and quesadillas, all made to order with fresh ingredients.

Zambrero is notable for its Plate 4 Plate programme, which donates a meal to someone in need for every burrito or bowl sold. Damian Bennett, development agent for Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire, expressed excitement about bringing fresh Mexican flavours to the area, stating, "We’re thrilled to bring fresh, feel-good Mexican flavours to Rochdale."

The menu caters to various dietary preferences, including vegetarian, vegan, and halal options, allowing customers to fully customise their meals. This initiative not only aims to satisfy local diners but also contributes to tackling world hunger through its charitable programme.

The opening of Zambrero is expected to enhance the dining options available in Rochdale, providing residents with a new place to enjoy quality Mexican cuisine while also supporting a good cause. Customers can visit the restaurant to experience the new offerings and participate in the Plate 4 Plate initiative.

articles.title: Medequip Secures Community Equipment Loan Service Contract for Rochdale and Surrounding Areas
articles.excerpt: Medequip has been awarded a contract to provide the Community Equipment Loan Service for Rochdale, Oldham, Stockport, and Tameside, starting on 1 October 2026.
articles.content_html:
Community equipment services provider Medequip has been awarded the contract to deliver the Community Equipment Loan Service (CELS) for Rochdale, Oldham, Stockport, and Tameside. This contract, awarded by a partnership of the four local authorities and the NHS Greater Manchester Integrated Care Board (ICB), will commence on 1 October 2026 and will initially run for three years, with an option to extend for up to two additional years.

The CELS plays a crucial role in supporting both adults and children to live independently and safely at home. Medequip will manage the full lifecycle of community equipment, which includes procurement, delivery, installation, maintenance, repair, collection, decontamination, refurbishment, and recycling. This service is integral to the integrated health and social care systems, facilitating timely hospital discharges and preventing avoidable admissions.

As part of the transition to the new contract, Medequip will initially operate from its existing service depot in Dukinfield. Subsequently, the company plans to relocate to a new, purpose-built service centre within the Hollinwood Junction development. This modern facility, spanning 32,450 square feet, has been designed with sustainability in mind and will enhance operational capacity while ensuring efficient service delivery across the four boroughs.

The new service centre will support Medequip's commitment to providing high-quality services and maximising the collection, refurbishment, and reuse of equipment, aligning with sustainable circular economy principles. This development is expected to significantly benefit residents in Rochdale and the surrounding areas, ensuring they have access to necessary equipment to maintain their independence.

articles.title: Two Boys Seriously Injured in E-Bike Crash on Windermere Road, Middleton
articles.excerpt: A serious collision involving an e-bike and a car on Windermere Road in Middleton has left two boys, aged 13 and 14, in hospital with serious injuries. A man in his 20s has been arrested in connection with the incident.
articles.content_html:
Two boys were rushed to hospital following a serious collision between an e-bike and a car in Middleton. The incident occurred on Windermere Road, at the junction with Wood Street, at approximately 8pm on Monday, September 28, 2026.

Emergency services, including a large number of police and paramedic vehicles, responded to the scene. A cordon was established across a stretch of the road while crews worked to assist the injured and investigate the circumstances of the crash. The boys, aged 13 and 14, were reported to have sustained serious injuries and were taken to hospital for treatment.

The driver of the car, a man in his 20s, was arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by driving without due care and attention. He has since been taken into custody for questioning. The road remained closed for several hours as officers from Greater Manchester Police's Serious Collision Investigation Unit conducted their inquiries, with evidence markers placed on the road within the cordon.

Police are now seeking information from the public regarding the incident. They urge anyone who witnessed the crash or has footage to come forward. Information can be reported to Greater Manchester Police by calling 101 and quoting log 3478 of September 28, 2026, or via the LiveChat function on their website. Alternatively, reports can be made anonymously to Crimestoppers at 0800 555 111.

articles.title: High Court Trial Begins Over Ownership of Hopwood Hall
articles.excerpt: A two-day trial in Manchester will determine the future of Hopwood Hall as Hopwood DePree seeks to reclaim his ancestral home from Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
The High Court in Manchester has commenced a two-day trial concerning the ownership of Hopwood Hall, a historic manor house in Rochdale. The case pits Hopwood DePree against Rochdale Council, as Mr DePree seeks to restore his ancestral home, which has been in disrepair for decades.

Mr DePree, a descendant of the Hopwood family who built the manor in the 1420s, claims that the council reneged on an agreement allowing him to purchase the property. The Hopwood family owned the hall and its surrounding land, now part of Hopwood Hall College, until 1922. Following its sale in 1942, the hall was used for various purposes, including as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s, before being acquired by Rochdale Council.

The legal dispute arose after Mr DePree spent seven years collaborating with the council on necessary repairs to the site, with the intention of purchasing it. However, in November 2024, the council ended its exclusivity agreement with him, stating that no commercially viable business model had been presented. Mr DePree argues that the council's decision violates the terms of their agreement, particularly after planning permission was granted in 2022.

The outcome of this trial could significantly impact the future of Hopwood Hall, which is currently a Grade II-listed property. A ruling in favour of Mr DePree may lead to the restoration of the hall, while a decision for the council could open the door for alternative plans for the site.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the local verb “cruckle”: what it means, where it comes from, and why people in Rochdale still call that awkward ankle‑twist by its own name.
articles.summary: A short guide to the local verb “cruckle”: what it means, where it comes from, and why people in Rochdale still call that awkward ankle‑twist by its own name.
articles.body:
If you grew up in parts of Rochdale you will probably recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” Locally, to “cruckle” means to roll or twist an ankle — the small, nasty half‑twist you can often walk off but that still makes you wince. That is the everyday sense people in the borough use now, and it is the reason the word still turns up in conversation, social media and local memory.

How old is the word? It is not a modern invention. Historical dialect lexicons record a family of related words — crookle, crug, cruggle and similar forms — with meanings in the same semantic field (to bend, make crooked, crouch, hobble). These entries show the shape of an older northern and Scots dialect pattern in which a crook/krug root combines with a frequentative or verbalising ending (‑le) to make verbs that suggest bending or awkward movement. The Dictionary of the Scots Language lists cruggle/cruckle/krukel and cites quotations from the late 19th and early 20th centuries showing meanings such as “to crouch” or “to huddle.”

Is “cruckle” uniquely Rochdale? That depends on how you measure uniqueness. On the one hand, historical records show related forms elsewhere in northern England and in Scots dialects: the root and word‑building pattern are regional rather than invented in a single street. On the other hand, folk‑linguistic evidence — what people themselves say about local speech — ties the word strongly to Rochdale today. A recent perceptual‑dialect study of Greater Manchester (published 2024) collected hundreds of crowd‑sourced “draw‑a‑map” responses and keyword comments; among the words respondents associated with Rochdale was “cruckle,” listed alongside other locally salient items such as “guinnel” (ginnel). That kind of data shows a living social association: speakers and listeners link the term particularly with Rochdale speech.

Why does that combination (regional history + local claim) happen? Dialect words survive or disappear for lots of reasons — local mobility, schooling, media influence, and family speech habits all matter — but certain small words endure because they carry social meaning. A term like cruckle does two jobs at once: it names a familiar action, and it signals belonging. Perceptual dialect research treats items like this as useful indicators of both language change (who still uses the word) and language attitude (which words people believe mark their place).

What can dialect research tell us beyond smells of nostalgia? Two lessons stand out. First, forms such as cruckle fit predictable historical patterns (crook/krug + ‑le) that linguists have documented across northern English and Scots; that explains why related words appear in different places and times. Second, modern mapping and keyword studies show that local recognition — not just historical presence — determines whether words feel “from” a place. In Rochdale’s case, continued local use and local identification appear to have made cruckle feel distinctly Rochdale even while similar forms exist elsewhere.

A final practical note: it is difficult to prove absolute exclusivity for any dialect word. Administrative borders do not stop words from spreading, and historical records sometimes show wider distribution than folk memory suggests. What we can say, on the basis of published dialect lexicons and a 2024 perceptual study, is this: cruckle has roots in older northern dialect vocabulary, and today it is strongly associated with Rochdale in people’s perceptions and daily talk. If you have family spellings, old letters or recorded uses of the word, local archives and dialect projects welcome contributions — small words like this are precisely the material researchers need to trace how language and place stay entwined.

A High Court hearing is scheduled for tomorrow, September 29, concerning a dispute between Hollywood actor Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council regarding the future of the historic Hopwood Hall in Middleton. The case arises after the council terminated its exclusivity agreement with DePree at the end of 2024, which had allowed him to lead the redevelopment of the Grade II*-listed site.

DePree, who has claimed to have invested over £750,000 in the restoration of Hopwood Hall, argues that he has a legally binding agreement to purchase the property. The council, however, contends that the agreement was ended due to insufficient progress on the project and the need to explore other investment opportunities. Following the termination, the site was closed to volunteers due to alleged health and safety breaches, according to the council.

The upcoming trial at the Manchester Civil Justice Centre will determine whether the council is obligated to transfer ownership of Hopwood Hall to DePree. His Honour Judge Hodge KC will preside over the two-day proceedings, during which both parties will present their arguments.

The outcome of this case could significantly impact the future of Hopwood Hall, a site with historical significance dating back to the 1400s. DePree has expressed hope that the court will rule in his favour, allowing him to continue his efforts to restore the building.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Launches Increased Parking Patrols Outside Schools
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has launched a new campaign to improve safety for schoolchildren by increasing parking enforcement outside schools and reminding drivers to stop for crossing patrols.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has initiated a new campaign titled “Stop Means Stop” aimed at enhancing safety for schoolchildren by reminding drivers of their responsibilities at school crossing patrols. The campaign was launched by Councillor Dylan Williams, the council’s cabinet member for Highways and Facilities, at St Luke’s Primary School in Heywood.

As part of the campaign, the council announced that parking enforcement patrols outside schools will be increased. This decision follows the recording of 137 instances over the past five years where drivers failed to stop for school crossing patrols, including cases where patrols had already stepped into the road. Councillor Williams highlighted the dangers posed to children, stating, “This is obviously a real danger for schoolchildren across the borough. It’s really important that people stop.”

In addition to the increased patrols, the council is urging drivers to keep yellow lines and school keep-clear markings free of parked vehicles. A crossing patrol worker at St Luke’s, identified as Chris, noted that vehicles parked on zigzag lines obstructed both his view and the view of passing drivers, which could lead to dangerous situations.

The increased parking patrols will not follow a fixed schedule, allowing for flexibility in enforcement. A parent at St Luke’s Primary School suggested that families should consider parking further away to leave space clear near the crossing, contributing to a safer environment for children. The council’s efforts aim to foster a safer atmosphere for schoolchildren as they arrive and depart from school.

This decision, made on Friday, is part of a broader strategy to stimulate regeneration across the northern regions of Greater Manchester.

The Rochdale MDC will focus on revitalising key areas within the borough, with plans to deliver 2,000 new homes and community facilities across six sites. The initiative is expected to attract investment and improve local infrastructure, although specific project details are still to be confirmed.

This approval follows the successful implementation of a similar MDC in Stockport, which has been credited with driving significant development in that area. The GMCA aims to replicate this success in Rochdale and the other boroughs involved, fostering economic growth and community enhancement.

Next steps will involve detailed planning and consultation with local stakeholders to ensure that the development meets the needs of residents and businesses in Rochdale. The GMCA's commitment to these projects signals a proactive approach to addressing local challenges and promoting sustainable development in the region.

articles.excerpt: Councillor Lee Wolf has requested an urgent meeting with police and council officers following reports of disorder in Middleton town centre and at the former Durnford Street School site, urging immediate action to address the situation.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

20:57, 28 September 2026

Councillor Lee Wolf has requested an urgent meeting with police and council officers following reports of disorder in Middleton town centre and at the former Durnford Street School site, urging immediate action to ensure community safety.

Councillor Lee Wolf has called for an urgent meeting with Greater Manchester Police and council officers in response to increasing reports of disorder in Middleton town centre and at the former Durnford Street School site. In a post on a local Facebook group, he expressed concern that the area could become a 'no-go zone' for residents if immediate action is not taken.

Councillor Wolf highlighted that groups of young people have been entering the former school site daily, climbing onto its roof and throwing stones and mud at passing and parked vehicles. He noted that some parents have even dropped their children off at the site, which he described as inadequately secured. He is advocating for the installation of surveillance cameras at the location, including those capable of capturing vehicle registration plates.

In his post, Councillor Wolf urged residents to report every incident to the police to ensure there is an official record of the disturbances. Local residents have echoed his concerns, with reports of dangerous behaviour including a cyclist in a balaclava nearly colliding with a pedestrian and fireworks being directed towards shops and cars. Other incidents included fireworks being set off in bins outside businesses, and young people reportedly throwing fireworks and entering food shops near Tesco.

The councillor's call for action comes amid growing unease in the community regarding safety in the town centre. The meeting he has requested aims to address these issues directly with police and council officials, seeking a coordinated response to restore safety and security for residents.

articles.title: Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel: rock, history and the stories that grew around them
articles.excerpt: A riverside alcove called the Fairies’ Chapel is very real — the fairies that haunt it belong to a long local storytelling tradition rather than to the record of verifiable events.
articles.summary: A riverside alcove called the Fairies’ Chapel is very real — the fairies that haunt it belong to a long local storytelling tradition rather than to the record of verifiable events.
articles.body:
Stand for a moment by the narrow cleft of the Thrutch in Healey Dell and it is easy to see why people once spoke of a tiny chapel for otherworldly visitors. The River Spodden has cut a pulpit‑like niche and benches from the rock; the cleft, the surrounding mill remains and the dramatic Victorian viaduct are the things you can point to, map and photograph.

Those are the documented facts. Healey Dell is managed and described by Rochdale Borough Council as a nature reserve and visitor site with woodland, waterfalls, mill remains and a heritage centre. The Dell’s high railway viaduct — an important visible landmark — is recorded as a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England; the listing notes the viaduct dates from 1869–70 (listing first entered on 30 November 1984). The Healey Dell Heritage Centre and local walking guides explain the site’s industrial archaeology and contemporary visitor facilities. (Rochdale Borough Council; Historic England).

Where the fairies come in lies in printed and oral tradition rather than council minutes or building records. The best known early printed account of Healey’s supernatural associations appears in John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (first published in the early nineteenth century), which collects versions of local romances and legends that include a “Fairies’ Chapel,” a miller, witches, a Fairy Queen and a small “Healey Dwarf.” Later nineteenth‑ and twentieth‑century local writers and the Dell’s own heritage materials repeat and retell those stories, sometimes in verse or in fanciful narrative form.

Local heritage interpretation explains the likely practical origin of the name. The “chapel” was a natural water‑eroded hollow at the base of the Thrutch that resembled an altar, pulpit and seats; Victorian tourists and local storytellers read human and sacred forms into these shapes and linked them to earlier folk beliefs. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre guide also records that a violent flood on 4 July 1838 reshaped parts of the Dell and destroyed some features previously associated with the chapel — underlining how the landscape itself, through erosion and flood, has altered the things people once saw there.

That combination of physical feature plus long local storytelling explains why modern references to a “Fairies’ Chapel” mix geology, industrial history and folklore. The accounts in Roby and in local guides are valuable as records of what people once believed and told; they are not contemporary evidence that supernatural beings exist. Claims that a Fairy King, witches’ covens, or a living Healey Dwarf actually inhabit the Dell are part of that folklore tradition and cannot be verified by archival records or official sources.

For residents and visitors the place works on two levels at once: as a real, protected landscape with listed industrial structures and as a pocket of cultural memory that has gathered tales for centuries. The Dell’s heritage displays, family trails and the local “Fairy Grotto” acknowledge that storytelling role while the council and Historic England listings record the concrete, documented elements of the site.

If you come to Healey Dell, bring both a torch for the paths and a readiness to listen. Treat the Fairies’ Chapel as a striking example of how landscape and local imagination meet — an important piece of our borough’s natural and cultural heritage, whether or not you believe in fairies.

(If you want to read the earliest printed versions of the Healey tales, consult John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire; for the site’s current description and visitor information see Rochdale Borough Council’s Healey Dell entry and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre materials.)

articles.title: Rochdale Council Launches 'Stop Means Stop' Campaign to Protect Children on School Runs
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has initiated a campaign to improve safety for children during school runs, focusing on the importance of stopping for school crossing patrols and enforcing parking restrictions outside schools.
articles.content_html:
A new campaign aimed at improving safety for children during school runs has been launched by Rochdale Council. The initiative, named the 'Stop Means Stop' campaign, was introduced last week at St Luke’s Primary School in Heywood. The campaign seeks to remind drivers of their responsibility to stop for school crossing patrols, particularly as children return to school after the holidays.

Councillor Dylan Williams, the cabinet member for Highways and Facilities, emphasised the importance of this message, stating that there have been 137 incidents of drivers failing to stop for patrols outside schools over the past five years. This alarming statistic highlights the need for increased awareness and adherence to road safety measures during school hours.

In addition to the campaign, parking wardens will be deployed more frequently around schools to enforce parking restrictions. Councillor Williams noted that improper parking outside schools significantly reduces visibility, increasing the risk of accidents involving children. He urged drivers to be more considerate and to leave adequate space around schools during drop-off and pick-up times.

The 'Stop Means Stop' campaign is part of a broader effort to ensure the safety of children in the borough. As the school year progresses, residents can expect to see heightened enforcement of parking regulations and ongoing reminders about the importance of road safety around schools.

Greater Manchester Police have initiated a murder investigation following the death of a 44-year-old woman discovered at a property on Tweedale Street in Rochdale on 25 May 2026.

14:55, 27 September 2026

A Festival of Remembrance will take place at Rochdale Town Hall on October 16, recognising the service and sacrifice of armed forces personnel, with proceeds supporting local charities.

A Festival of Remembrance will be held at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday, October 16, to pay tribute to members of the armed forces community, both past and present. The event will feature performances by military bands, an act of remembrance, and the sharing of historic war stories, providing an opportunity for attendees to reflect and reminisce.

The Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, will be among the guests, alongside Members of Parliament, councillors, and dignitaries from across the Armed Forces. Councillor Rana expressed that the evening will be a special occasion for the Armed Forces community to unite in honouring the bravery and sacrifices made by service personnel.

Funds raised during the event will be directed towards the Mayor of Rochdale’s charities for the 2026/27 period. The beneficiaries include The Rochdale Veterans Breakfast Club, Rochdale Women’s Welfare Association, SANDS (Stillbirth and Neonatal Death Society), Springhill Hospice, and The Christie.

This event not only serves as a remembrance but also aims to foster community spirit and support for local charities, making it a significant occasion for Rochdale residents.
